chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Saeed, from Musaddaq ibn Sadaqa, from Ammar al-Sabati, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

He was asked about raisins, how to cook them so that their drink is permissible. He said: 'Take a quarter of raisins, clean them, then pour twelve ratls of water over them, then soak them overnight. When it is the next day, remove their foam, then pour water over them sufficient to submerge them, then boil them with fire until they boil, then remove their water and pour it over the first water.'

Then place it all in one vessel, then light a fire beneath it until two-thirds of it evaporates and one-third remains, with the fire still beneath it. Then take a ratl of honey, boil it with fire until it boils, and remove its foam. Then place it upon the cooked mixture, then stir it until it mixes with it. And if you wish, add saffron to it, and if you wish, flavor it with a little ginger.

He said: 'So if you want to divide it into three parts to cook it, measure it with one thing until you know how much it is. Then place the first part in the vessel in which you boil it, then make a measurement and mark it where the water reaches. Then place the other third, then mark it where the water reaches. Then place the final third, then mark it where the last one reaches. Then ignite a gentle fire beneath it until two-thirds of it evaporates and one-third remains.'
ai.seo_question: How to prepare raisin drink so it is halal according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the precise culinary and legal methodology for preparing 'Zabib' (raisin drink/vinegar) by Imam al-Sadiq (AS), emphasizing the control of fermentation through specific boiling and reduction ratios to ensure it remains Halal. It reflects the Shia scholarly tradition of linking practical domestic arts with fiqh, illustrating how minor variations in preparation can determine the permissibility of consumables. The inclusion of honey and optional spices like saffron or ginger highlights the balance between preservation, taste, and ritual purity in early Islamic society.
